title: Geometric Causal Models
hook: Causal inference usually assumes i.i.d. data. This framework builds causal models around the symmetries data actually has — spatial, network, genomic — unlocking inference where classical methods don't apply.
key_points: Geometric causal models (GCMs) exploit symmetries — translation-invariance in spatial data, permutation-invariance in graphs — to enable causal identification on dependent, non-i.i.d. data.
Formalizes symmetry with group theory, then uses ergodic theory for amenable groups to establish when causal effects are identifiable at all.
Recovers standard i.i.d. causal models and do-calculus as the special case where the symmetry is just permutation over a sequence.
Constructs a GCM matching DNA's own symmetries, combining deep genomics models with DNA language models to estimate effects of genetic variation.
content_html: A lot of real-world data that scientists want to draw causal conclusions from — spatial measurements, social networks, molecular structures — isn't independent and identically distributed, the assumption baked into most causal-inference machinery. Geometric causal models offer a way around that constraint by building the model around the data's actual symmetries instead.
extra_html: Eli Weinstein and David Blei formalize a data-generating process's symmetries with group theory: translation-invariance for spatial data, permutation-invariance for graph data, or other structures depending on the domain. Ergodic theory for amenable groups tells them when causal effects are identifiable at all under a given symmetry, and geometric deep learning combined with scalable Bayesian inference handles estimation. When the symmetry is just permutation equivariance over a sequence, the framework recovers familiar i.i.d. causal models and do-calculus — showing GCMs generalize rather than replace standard causal inference. As a concrete demonstration, they construct a GCM matching the symmetries of DNA itself, pairing deep functional-genomics models (for outcomes) with DNA language models (for propensities) to estimate the effects of genetic variation, illustrated on semisynthetic data. Eli N. Weinstein and David M. Blei, arXiv 2026.

related.title: Deep Double Descent
related.hook: Bigger models should overfit, then get worse — right? Instead test error often dips, climbs, then dips again as model size grows, breaking the classic bias-variance story.

related.title: The Bias–Variance Tradeoff
related.hook: Too simple and your model misses the pattern; too flexible and it chases noise. Generalization lives between the two.

flashcards.prompt: What data assumption does classical causal inference typically require, and what do geometric causal models replace it with?
flashcards.back_html: Classical causal inference typically assumes independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) data. Geometric causal models instead exploit the actual symmetries of dependent data — like translation-invariance in space or permutation-invariance in graphs — to make causal inference possible.

flashcards.prompt: What happens to standard i.i.d. causal models under the geometric causal models (GCM) framework?

choices.text: They fall out as a special case, when the data is a sequence and the symmetry is permutation equivariance
They become invalid and must be discarded
They only apply to spatial data, never to sequences
GCMs replace do-calculus entirely with a new incompatible framework

flashcards.explanation_html: GCMs generalize rather than replace: when the symmetry is permutation equivariance over a sequence, the framework recovers the familiar i.i.d. causal models and do-calculus as one instance of a broader family.
